title: Non-Commutative
body:
An operation is **non-commutative** when the order of its operands changes the answer.
[[Matrix Multiplication]] is the course's example: **$AB \neq BA$ in general**.

Three separate ways it fails, from cheapest to most interesting:

1. **$BA$ may not exist.** $A$ is $2 \times 3$, $B$ is $3 \times 4$: $AB$ is fine, $BA$ has
   mismatched inner dimensions and is undefined.
2. **$BA$ may exist with a different shape.** $A$ is $2 \times 3$, $B$ is $3 \times 2$: $AB$ is
   $2 \times 2$ and $BA$ is $3 \times 3$. Not even comparable.
3. **Both may be square and equal in shape, and still differ.** $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4
   \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 19 & 22 \\ 43 &
   50 \end{bmatrix}$, while the reverse product is $\begin{bmatrix} 23 & 34 \\ 31 & 46
   \end{bmatrix}$.

The reason is in [[Matrix Multiplication]]: a matrix is a [[Linear Transformation]] and the
product is function composition. Rotating then reflecting is not reflecting then rotating.

Matrices that *do* commute are the exception and each one is worth noticing: anything with $I$,
anything with a scalar multiple of itself, $A$ with $A^{-1}$, and two diagonal matrices. The
last is a large part of why [[Diagonalization]] is worth the effort.

Note that matrix **addition** is perfectly commutative. It is only multiplication that breaks.
